newsitem.title: INDIA: India sugar trade calls for price deregulation.
newsitem.headline: India sugar trade calls for price deregulation.

text.p: India must deregulate sugar prices to minimise fluctuations in output and protect domestic industry from high production costs, its sugar traders say.
"We are again reiterating our stand for decontrol of the sugar sector," M. Manickam, president of the Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA), told reporters late on Friday in the Indian capital.
"A long-term policy of decontrol of sugar prices will help stabilise the sugar economy," Manickam said.

Sugar production and pricing in India are controlled by the government. The mills supply 40 percent of their output at a subsidised rate for distribution among the poor. The government controls the release of the remainder in the free market through the use of sales quotas.
ISMA officials said under the current rules, the industry is forced to supply sugar to the poor at prices which are set by the government and are often below the cost of production.
Manickam said the international price of sugarcane was about 550 rupees ($15.4) per tonne but in India, sugarcane cost the millers about 750 rupees.
"Global cost of production is much lower," Manickam said. "We are handicapped by the high cane prices."
Manickam said India's sugar output in the 1997/98 (October-September) season was expected to dip sharply to 10.5 million tonnes from 12.8 million in 1996/97.
"The output might touch 11 million tonnes if government policies change," he said.
Manickam said much of the area under sugarcane was expected to be diverted to other crops because sugar farmers got low prices for their produce in the current season.
"We expect a lot of crop diversion because farmers got better prices in this season in crops such as wheat," he added.
But India will not face a sugar shortage in 1997/98 because it would start the season with carryover stocks of 6.6 million tonnes, Manickam said.
He said the industry feared large scale sugar imports as traders found importing sugar cheaper than growing it.

"Some checks and balances must be introduced on imported sugar rather than leaving it completely free," Manickam said. He urged the government to impose a countervailing duty of 30 percent on sugar imports.

He said India had the potential to export up to 2.5 million tonnes of sugar and to earn 25 billion rupees in foreign exchange annually due to its strategic location, surrounded by major sugar importing countries in the world.
"But proper incentives have to be given by the government," Manickam said. He did not elaborate.
India in January ended the monopoly of Indian Sugar and General Industry Export-Import Corp, a private corporation set up by the sugar milling industry, over exports of sugar.

The decision was considered an important step towards freeing the sugar industry from a decades-old system of licensing, pricing and distribution. But exports have not picked up due to high domestic prices. ($1 = 35.7 rupees)
